newsitem.title: USA: Negotiators seek end to San Francisco garbage strike.
newsitem.headline: Negotiators seek end to San Francisco garbage strike.

text.p: Striking garbage collectors and managers held talks Friday to try to resolve a two-day-old strike for higher wages that has caused trash to pile up at homes across San Francisco.
More than 500 garbage collectors went on strike Thursday in a dispute over a new labor contract. It is San Francisco's first such strike in 57 years.
Garbage company managers collected trash from hospitals, hotels, businesses and schools, but they were not picking up from homes, where garbage started to pile up.
Mayor Willie Brown has indicated he may declare a local state of emergency if there was evidence that the strike posed a threat to the health or public safety of San Franciscans.

But, with talks between strikers and management still going on, Brown said late Friday that he had decided not to declare an emergency for now. "The evidence is not yet there to justify a state of emergency," he told a packed news conference.
An emergency would allow Brown to call out city workers to pick up trash, but local labor leaders said it was wrong to expect public employees to serve as strike breakers.
Management and union leaders met for a second day to try to break the deadlock but there was no word if they were making any progress. The talks were expected to continue until late Friday.

Union leaders called the strike after workers rejected the latest contract offer by Sunset Scavenger Co. and Golden Gate Disposal & Recycling Co., subsidiaries of Norcal Waste Systems Inc., which collect the city's garbage.
The striking garbage collectors had worked without a contract since Dec. 31. Union officials said the workers would stay off the job for as long as necessary.
City officials, fearing a prolonged strike could pose health risks, advised residents not to put garbage out on the curb.

Workers are seeking a three-year contract, an 80-cents-per-hour pay increase, an early retirement plan and improved health benefits. The average garbage truck driver now earns $20.58 per hour or $49,000 a year.

Norcal said its latest proposal to striking workers would boost their pay by 13.3 percent over five years, and increase health care and pension benefits. "We can't afford to put anything else on the table," Norcal president Michael Sangiacomo said.
